title: Saudi Arabia for First-Timers: AlUla, Diriyah and the Red Sea
metaDescription: A practical first-visit guide to Saudi Arabia — AlUla’s rock-cut tombs, Diriyah, Jeddah’s old town and Red Sea diving, plus visas, dress and etiquette.
excerpt: Saudi Arabia opened to tourists recently and most people still have no idea what is there. The short answer: Nabataean tombs, an untouched Red Sea, and mountains.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
Saudi Arabia issued its first tourist visas only recently, which means most travellers' mental image of the country is either entirely blank or built from news coverage. What is actually there surprises people: rock-cut Nabataean tombs comparable to Petra, a Red Sea coastline with reefs barely touched by tourism, mountain villages at 2,500 metres, and a vast, genuinely empty desert.

It is also an expensive, conservative country in the middle of a rapid and highly visible transformation, and going with clear expectations matters more than usual.

## Getting In

Most nationalities can now apply for an **e-visa online** or obtain a visa on arrival, valid for a year with multiple entries and stays up to 90 days. The process is quick and mandatory health insurance is bundled into the fee.

A few notes:

- **Mecca is closed to non-Muslims.** Medina's central area likewise. This is absolute
- **The tourist visa does not permit Hajj**, though it can be used for Umrah by Muslim travellers at permitted times
- **Alcohol is illegal** throughout the country. There are no exceptions for tourists, hotels or expatriate compounds

![Saudi Arabia travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1584551246679-0daf3d275d0f?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## AlUla: The Reason to Go

If you visit one place in Saudi Arabia, this is it.

**Hegra (Madain Salih)** is the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Site and the southern city of the Nabataean kingdom — the same civilisation that built Petra. More than a hundred monumental tombs carved into sandstone outcrops, standing in open desert. Unlike Petra, you will frequently have a tomb entirely to yourself.

The surrounding area holds more:

- **Dadan and Jabal Ikmah** — an older kingdom's site, with a canyon of ancient inscriptions described as an open-air library
- **AlUla Old Town** — a mudbrick settlement being carefully restored
- **Elephant Rock** — a natural formation, best at sunset
- **The oasis** — date palms and a genuinely lovely walking trail

AlUla is managed as a curated destination, with timed tickets and official guides for Hegra. Book ahead in high season. It is also where Saudi's most striking new hotels are, and they are priced accordingly.

**Go between November and March.** Summer temperatures make the site unvisitable in the middle of the day.

## Diriyah and Riyadh

**Diriyah**, on Riyadh's edge, is the mudbrick birthplace of the Saudi state — a restored district of earthen architecture that is being developed into a major heritage quarter. At-Turaif is UNESCO-listed and worth a half day.

**Riyadh** itself is a modern capital rather than a historic one. The National Museum is genuinely good, Edge of the World — a dramatic escarpment about 90 minutes out — is the best day trip, and the old Masmak Fortress and Diriyah cover the history.

Riyadh is a business city that has become more open, with a rapidly expanding restaurant and entertainment scene. It is not, on its own, a compelling tourist destination.

## Jeddah and the Red Sea

**Jeddah** is the more relaxed, more cosmopolitan counterweight to Riyadh. **Al-Balad**, the old town, is a UNESCO-listed district of coral-stone merchant houses with carved wooden balconies, undergoing restoration and best explored on foot in the evening. The corniche is long and pleasant.

**The Red Sea coast** is Saudi Arabia's genuinely world-class natural asset. The reefs north of Jeddah and around Yanbu are in excellent condition with minimal diving pressure. Liveaboards run along the coast. Large resort developments are under construction on the northern coast, which will change this — currently it is one of the least-dived healthy reef systems in the world.

![Saudi Arabia travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1575538439014-1b8bc5fcaa1d?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The Mountains and the South

The least-visited and, for many travellers, the most interesting region.

**Asir province**, in the southwest, is a different country climatically — mountains above 2,500 metres, green, cool, and with a distinct architecture of stone towers and painted interiors. **Rijal Almaa** is a stone village of stacked buildings; **Abha** is the regional hub; the escarpment roads and cable cars are dramatic.

**Taif** sits in the mountains above Mecca — cooler, known for roses, and reachable from Jeddah.

If you have more than a week, this region is what separates a Saudi trip from a monuments-and-cities itinerary.

## Practicalities and Etiquette

**Dress.** Women are no longer legally required to wear an abaya, and foreign women generally do not. Modest dress is expected: covered shoulders and knees, loose clothing. A headscarf is not required except in mosques. Men should avoid shorts in public.

**Behaviour.** Public displays of affection are not acceptable. Photography of people, especially women, without permission is a serious matter. Prayer times close some shops briefly, five times a day — plan around it rather than being caught out.

**Ramadan.** Eating, drinking or smoking in public during daylight hours is prohibited and enforced. Visiting during Ramadan is possible but changes the trip substantially.

**LGBTQ+ travellers** should be aware that same-sex relationships are criminalised. This is a serious legal risk, not a cultural nuance.

**Women travelling alone** can now travel, book hotels and move freely. Many solo female travellers report positive experiences, alongside a level of attention and curiosity that can be wearing.

## Getting Around and Costs

**Domestic flights** connect the main cities cheaply and frequently; the country is large and driving between regions is a serious undertaking. The **Haramain high-speed rail** links Jeddah, Mecca, Medina and KAEC.

**Renting a car** is the best way to see AlUla and the south. Roads are excellent. Women may drive.

**Costs** are high by regional standards: budget $80–120 a day, mid-range $180–280, and considerably more for AlUla's signature hotels. There is very little budget accommodation infrastructure.

## A Ten-Day First Visit

- **Days 1–2** — Riyadh and Diriyah, with Edge of the World
- **Days 3–5** — AlUla: Hegra, Dadan, the old town, the oasis
- **Days 6–7** — Jeddah and Al-Balad
- **Days 8–10** — either Red Sea diving from Jeddah or Yanbu, or fly south to Abha and Asir

## Should You Go?

If you want Petra-scale archaeology without the crowds, healthy reefs, and a country that very few people you know have visited, yes — and sooner rather than later, because AlUla and the Red Sea coast are being developed rapidly.

Go understanding what you are visiting: a conservative country with laws considerably stricter than most travellers are used to, undergoing a fast, state-driven transformation. Travellers who go with that understanding tend to come back genuinely impressed. Travellers who expect Dubai with ruins do not.

Distances here are large and domestic flights structure the trip, so the sequencing matters more than usual. Laying out the legs and the fixed bookings — Hegra tickets especially — in a shared plan on **Trypinn** before you book flights will save you an expensive backtrack.
